intro: This is real Rust — the same language used in servers, games and operating systems. The One Dollar Computer runs a small, honest part of it. Ten tiny lessons: read one, run it, change it. Everything you learn here works in full Rust.

concept: Every Rust program starts in a function called main. The computer reads it from the first line to the last.
loop repeats the lines inside it forever — exactly what a small computer should do: turn the light on, wait, turn it off, wait, again.
lessons.title: A program: fn main and loop
lessons.try: Change both 200s to 500. The blink slows down — the numbers are milliseconds.

concept: let gives a name to a value: let wait = 500;

In Rust, a value cannot change after that — unless you say so with mut (short for mutable). This is Rust's first big idea: nothing changes behind your back. If a value can change, the code says it out loud.
lessons.title: Values that change: let and mut
lessons.try: The blink starts slow, then stays fast — because wait becomes 100 and never goes back. Change wait = 100 to wait = 50 and watch it speed up sooner.

concept: A value is never just a number — it has a type. u32 means a whole number that is never negative, big enough for 4 billion.

delay asks for a u32 of milliseconds. Rust checks types before the program runs and never converts them in secret. Writing the type is optional here (Rust can guess it), but seeing it once teaches you it is always there.
lessons.title: Every value has a type
lessons.try: Make a heartbeat: a short flash, a short pause, another short flash, then a long rest. You only need the two values and two more lines.

concept: if runs its lines only when the condition is true. else covers the other case.
Here the program counts blinks. While the count is small, the pause is short; when it reaches 5, the pause is long and the count starts again.
lessons.title: Deciding: if and else
lessons.try: Change count < 5 to count < 3. Now the long pause comes after three blinks instead of five.

concept: loop repeats forever. for repeats a counted number of times: 0..3 means 0, 1, 2 — three rounds.
while is the third way: it repeats while a condition stays true. Rust has all three because programs need all three.
lessons.title: Repeating a counted number of times: for
lessons.try: Change 0..3 to 0..5. The group now has five blinks before the long pause.

concept: A function is a named recipe. flash takes a value — ms, a u32 — and does the on-wait-off-wait with it.
Write the recipe once, use it with different values. main stays short and reads like a description of what the program does.
lessons.title: Your own recipes: functions
lessons.try: Add a fourth line, flash(1000);, before the loop closes. The rhythm gains a long final blink.

concept: match compares one value against a list of patterns and runs the matching one. _ catches everything else.
Rust checks that every possibility is covered — a case can never be forgotten silently. Programs read step 0, 1, 2 here as short, medium and long blinks.
lessons.title: Choosing between many: match
lessons.try: Delete the whole _ pattern and press Upload. Rust refuses and tells you a case is missing — that refusal is match protecting your program.

concept: An array holds several values of the same type, in order, with a size fixed when the program is written: [0, 1, 2, 3].
for can walk through an array one value at a time. Here four pins are prepared together, then lit one after another — a tiny chase light.
lessons.title: A fixed list of values: arrays
lessons.try: Add pin 4 to the list — and remember to change [u8; 4] to [u8; 5]. Rust checks the size you promised against the values you gave.

concept: Every value in Rust has exactly one owner. When a function takes a value, ownership moves into the function — the caller no longer has it.

blink_once takes the Blinker, uses it, and gives it back at the end, so main catches it again: led = blink_once(led). This one rule — one owner, moves are explicit, values are returned — is how Rust keeps programs safe without slowing them down. It is the heart of the language.
lessons.title: Who owns a value: ownership
lessons.try: Remove led = so the line is only blink_once(led); and press Upload. The compiler stops you: the Blinker moved in and never came back. Put led = back to fix it.

concept: Rust's compiler explains its errors like a teacher: what happened, exactly where, and often the fix. Reading the message is a programming skill — maybe the most useful one.

The classic first error: changing a value that was not declared mut. Rust answers "cannot assign twice to immutable variable" and adds "help: consider making this binding mutable". This program is the fixed version.
lessons.title: The compiler is a teacher
lessons.try: Delete the word mut, press Upload, and read the error slowly. Then fix it yourself by putting mut back. You just did what Rust programmers do every day.

title: Learn Rust
